title: Yeast permease and sugar isomers
stem: Galactose and glucose are monosaccharides that both have the molecular formula C6H12O6, but one hydroxyl group is oriented differently, so the two molecules have different three-dimensional shapes. A permease in the plasma membrane of yeast cells imports galactose far more slowly than it imports glucose. Which statement best explains why the permease can distinguish between the two sugars?

correct.text: The sugars contain the same atoms in different arrangements, so their shapes differ and only glucose fits the binding site of the permease well.
correct.rationale: The same atoms arranged differently give each sugar a distinct three-dimensional shape, and a transport protein binds the shape that fits its binding site.

wrong.text: The sugars contain different elements, so the permease binds glucose because it carries more atoms of carbon than galactose does.
wrong.rationale: Both sugars are C6H12O6, so they contain exactly the same numbers of every element; the proposed difference in atoms does not exist.
wrong.error_pattern: Believes isomers differ in atomic composition

wrong.text: Galactose is a lipid with a hydrophobic backbone, so the permease cannot move it through the membrane as quickly as glucose.
wrong.rationale: Galactose is a carbohydrate, not a lipid; it has many hydroxyl groups and is polar, so its identity as a monosaccharide matches glucose.

wrong.text: The sugars are joined by different types of covalent bonds, so the permease recognizes the sugar that has the stronger bonds.
wrong.rationale: Each sugar is a single monosaccharide; there are no bonds joining separate subunits, so bond type between monomers cannot explain the difference.
wrong.error_pattern: Applies polymer linkage ideas to monomers

change_note: New organism and sugar pair (galactose/glucose) with a transporter in yeast; shape-based recognition of isomers.

title: Receptor binding mirror-image molecules
stem: Spearmint and caraway oils contain two forms of carvone, a molecule with the formula C10H14O. The two forms have identical atoms and bonds but are mirror images of each other, so their three-dimensional shapes differ. A receptor protein in nasal cells binds one form strongly and the other only weakly. Which statement best explains this difference in binding?

correct.text: The forms have the same atoms but mirror-image arrangements, so only one shape fits the receptor's binding site closely.
correct.rationale: Mirror-image arrangement of identical atoms gives two shapes, and a receptor's binding site complements only one shape.

wrong.text: The forms have different molecular formulas, so the receptor binds the form that contains additional oxygen atoms.
wrong.rationale: The two forms have the same formula, C10H14O, so neither contains extra oxygen.

wrong.text: One form is a protein, so the receptor can bind it by using the side chains that are found only on amino acids.
wrong.rationale: Both forms are the same small molecule with identical atoms; neither is a protein, and no amino acid side chains are involved.

wrong.text: The forms differ in mass, so the receptor binds the heavier form because it moves more slowly toward the receptor.
wrong.rationale: Identical atoms give identical mass; binding depends on shape complementarity, not on how fast a molecule moves.

change_note: Different molecule type (carvone enantiomers) and a receptor rather than a transporter; same idea that shape determines binding.

title: Same amino acids different order
stem: Two tripeptides are made from the same three amino acids, alanine, glycine, and serine, but in the order Ala-Gly-Ser in one and Ser-Gly-Ala in the other. An antibody binds the first peptide strongly and the second one very weakly. Which statement best explains why the antibody can tell the two peptides apart?

correct.text: The peptides have the same composition but different sequences, so the groups are arranged differently in space and fit the antibody differently.
correct.rationale: Sequence order changes which R groups sit where, giving a different three-dimensional shape and surface for antibody binding.

wrong.text: The peptides contain different amino acids, so the antibody binds the peptide that has the larger number of different R groups.
wrong.rationale: Both peptides contain exactly the same three amino acids; only the order differs.

wrong.text: The peptides use different kinds of covalent linkages between subunits, so the antibody binds the one with peptide bonds.
wrong.rationale: Both peptides are linked by peptide bonds; the linkage type is identical.

wrong.text: The peptides have different total masses because order changes atoms, so the antibody binds the peptide with the greater mass.
wrong.rationale: Rearranging the order of the same amino acids does not change the number or kind of atoms, so the masses are equal.

change_note: Moves from sugar isomers to peptide sequence isomers; same principle that arrangement of identical atoms changes shape and recognition.

title: Surface leucine causes aggregation
stem: A mutation in a bacterial enzyme replaces a serine (polar, uncharged) on the protein's surface with leucine (nonpolar, hydrophobic). The mutant enzyme folds normally and remains active, but in water its molecules clump together into large aggregates, whereas the normal enzyme stays dispersed. Which best explains why the mutant molecules aggregate?

correct.text: The exposed nonpolar leucine side chains on separate molecules associate with each other to avoid water, linking the molecules through hydrophobic interactions.
correct.rationale: Hydrophobic side chains exposed on the surface cluster together away from water, so separate protein molecules stick together.

wrong.text: The leucine side chains form peptide bonds with neighboring enzyme molecules, joining the proteins into one large covalent polymer.
wrong.rationale: Peptide bonds form only between the amino group and carboxyl group of amino acids during translation; R groups do not form them with other proteins.
wrong.error_pattern: Confuses R-group interactions with peptide bonds

wrong.text: The leucine side chains form strong hydrogen bonds with water, which pulls the molecules together into aggregates.
wrong.rationale: Nonpolar side chains cannot form hydrogen bonds with water; serine, the polar residue that was replaced, could.

wrong.text: The leucine substitution adds a negative charge, so the neighboring molecules are attracted to each other by ionic bonds.
wrong.rationale: Leucine's side chain is nonpolar and uncharged, so it contributes no charge and no ionic attraction.
wrong.error_pattern: Assigns a charge to a nonpolar residue

change_note: New enzyme and a polar-to-nonpolar surface swap causing aggregation; no disease context.

title: Loss of ionic attraction between subunits
stem: Two subunits of a dimeric enzyme normally associate at an interface where aspartate 40 (negatively charged) on subunit A sits next to lysine 112 (positively charged) on subunit B. A mutation replaces lysine 112 with glutamate (negatively charged). The mutant subunits fold correctly but no longer form stable dimers. Which best explains the loss of dimer formation?

correct.text: The attraction between opposite charges is lost and the two negatively charged side chains now repel each other at the interface.
correct.rationale: Replacing the positive lysine with negative glutamate removes the ionic attraction and creates electrostatic repulsion.

wrong.text: The glutamate side chain forms a disulfide bond with aspartate 40, which locks the surface of subunit B in the wrong shape.
wrong.rationale: Glutamate and aspartate contain no sulfur, so neither can take part in a disulfide bond; disulfide bonds require cysteines.
wrong.error_pattern: Believes any charged residues form disulfides

wrong.text: The mutation breaks the peptide bond at position 112, so the subunit is cut in two and cannot reach the interface.
wrong.rationale: The substitution changes an R group only; the peptide bonds of the backbone remain intact and the subunit folds correctly.

wrong.text: Glutamate is nonpolar, so it moves into the core of the subunit and no longer faces the interface where it could bind.
wrong.rationale: Glutamate has a charged carboxyl side chain and is polar; it would not be buried like a nonpolar residue.

change_note: Tests R-group ionic interactions at a quaternary interface rather than hydrophobic polymerization; new protein and reversed charge logic.

title: Buried hydrophobic residue replaced by charged residue
stem: In a small globular enzyme, valine at position 73 is normally buried in the interior of the folded protein, surrounded by other nonpolar side chains. A mutation replaces valine 73 with aspartate, which has a negatively charged side chain. The mutant protein folds poorly and loses most of its activity at body temperature. Which best explains this effect?

correct.text: A charged side chain placed in the nonpolar interior cannot interact favorably with the surrounding nonpolar groups, destabilizing the folded tertiary structure.
correct.rationale: Charged groups are unstable in a hydrophobic core, so the protein's tertiary structure is disrupted.

wrong.text: Aspartate cannot form peptide bonds, so the polypeptide chain is cut at position 73 and the enzyme is shorter than normal.
wrong.rationale: Aspartate has the same amino and carboxyl groups as other amino acids and forms peptide bonds normally.
wrong.error_pattern: Believes some amino acids cannot form peptide bonds

wrong.text: The aspartate substitution changes the primary structure only, and primary structure has no effect on folding of the polypeptide.
wrong.rationale: The sequence of amino acids determines how the chain folds; changing one residue can alter tertiary structure.
wrong.error_pattern: Treats primary structure as irrelevant to folding

wrong.text: The negative charge of aspartate forms hydrogen bonds that are stronger than hydrophobic interactions and so improve stability.
wrong.rationale: A mismatch of a charged group in a nonpolar core lowers stability; the mutant is less stable, not more.
wrong.error_pattern: Assumes extra polar interactions always stabilize

change_note: Buried nonpolar to charged substitution tests tertiary structure stability; contrasts with seed's surface-exposed residue.

title: Cell classification with flagellum and chloroplast
stem: Two cells from a pond sample are examined by electron microscopy. Cell 1 is about 1 μm long, has a circular chromosome in a nucleoid region, 70S ribosomes, a flagellum, and no membrane-bound organelles. Cell 2 is about 15 μm long, has a nucleus, 80S ribosomes, chloroplasts, mitochondria, and a cellulose cell wall. Which conclusion is most directly supported by the observations?

correct.text: Cell 1 is prokaryotic because it lacks a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, and Cell 2 is eukaryotic because it has both.
correct.rationale: Absence of a nucleus and organelles marks a prokaryote; presence of a nucleus and organelles marks a eukaryote.

wrong.text: Cell 1 is eukaryotic because it has a flagellum, which is a structure found only in cells that contain membrane-bound organelles.
wrong.rationale: Prokaryotes can have flagella; a flagellum does not indicate eukaryotic classification.
wrong.error_pattern: Treats motility structure as eukaryote marker

wrong.text: Cell 2 is prokaryotic because it has a cell wall, and a cell wall is a feature that only prokaryotes possess.
wrong.rationale: Plants, fungi, and algae are eukaryotes with cell walls, so a wall does not indicate prokaryote status.
wrong.error_pattern: Believes cell walls occur only in prokaryotes

wrong.text: Both cells are prokaryotic because both are single cells living in the same pond and cannot be classified by structure.
wrong.rationale: Cells can be classified by structural features such as a nucleus, organelles, and ribosome type; habitat does not determine the cell type.
wrong.error_pattern: Classifies by habitat rather than structure

change_note: New cell pair (flagellated bacterium vs algal-type eukaryote) with distractors about flagella and walls.

title: Large prokaryote and small eukaryote
stem: A researcher compares two cells. Cell 1 is about 100 μm in diameter, has circular DNA free in the cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes, and no nucleus or other membrane-bound organelles. Cell 2 is about 8 μm in diameter, has a nucleus, mitochondria, 80S ribosomes, and a chitin cell wall. Which conclusion about the cells is most directly supported by the observations?

correct.text: Cell 1 is prokaryotic and Cell 2 is eukaryotic, because internal structure and not cell size separates the two types.
correct.rationale: Absence of a nucleus and organelles defines Cell 1 as prokaryotic despite its large size; Cell 2 has a nucleus and organelles.

wrong.text: Cell 1 is eukaryotic because its larger diameter shows that it must contain a nucleus and organelles to support its size.
wrong.rationale: Size does not determine classification; Cell 1 lacks a nucleus and organelles, so it is prokaryotic.

wrong.text: Cell 2 is prokaryotic because its small size and its cell wall are characteristics found only in prokaryotic cells.
wrong.rationale: Cell 2 has a nucleus and mitochondria, which define it as eukaryotic; small size and cell walls occur in both types.
wrong.error_pattern: Uses size and wall to classify

wrong.text: Both cells are prokaryotic because both have ribosomes and DNA, which are the only structures all cells need.
wrong.rationale: Ribosomes and DNA occur in both types; the nucleus, organelles, and 80S ribosomes show Cell 2 is eukaryotic.

change_note: Size reversed relative to seed (large prokaryote, small eukaryote) to test structural criteria over size.

title: Photosynthetic prokaryote versus alga
stem: Two photosynthetic cells are compared. Cell 1 is about 3 μm in diameter, has chlorophyll in folded membranes that are continuous with the plasma membrane, a circular chromosome in the cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes, and a peptidoglycan wall. Cell 2 is about 12 μm in diameter, has chloroplasts, a nucleus, and 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes. Which conclusion is most directly supported by the observations?

correct.text: Cell 1 is prokaryotic, although it carries out photosynthesis, and Cell 2 is eukaryotic because it has a nucleus and chloroplasts.
correct.rationale: Photosynthesis occurs in both types; lack of a nucleus and organelles indicates Cell 1 is prokaryotic.

wrong.text: Cell 1 is eukaryotic because photosynthesis can only be carried out in a cell that has membrane-bound chloroplasts.
wrong.rationale: Some prokaryotes photosynthesize using internal membrane folds without chloroplasts, so photosynthesis does not require eukaryotic organization.

wrong.text: Cell 2 is prokaryotic because it is photosynthetic, and only prokaryotic cells are able to capture light energy.
wrong.rationale: Chloroplasts and a nucleus show Cell 2 is eukaryotic, and eukaryotic algae and plants also capture light energy.
wrong.error_pattern: Believes light capture belongs to prokaryotes only

wrong.text: Both cells are eukaryotic because both contain membranes that hold chlorophyll, and only eukaryotes have membranes.
wrong.rationale: All cells have a plasma membrane; chlorophyll in membranes does not distinguish the types.

change_note: Photosynthesis as a distractor trap; cyanobacterium-like cell versus alga.

title: Potato core mass change in sucrose
stem: A student weighs a potato core, places it in 0.6 M sucrose for one hour, and reweighs it. The core's mass falls from 5.0 g to 4.3 g, a change of -14%, and the tissue feels limp. A core placed in distilled water instead gains mass and feels firm. Which best explains the limp tissue in 0.6 M sucrose?

correct.text: Water left the cells by osmosis because the sucrose solution was hypertonic, so turgor pressure fell and the tissue became limp.
correct.rationale: Net water moved out down its gradient, cytoplasm lost volume, and the loss of turgor made the tissue limp.

wrong.text: Sucrose entered the cells through the cell wall and replaced the cytoplasm, so the cells lost mass through exchange of sugar.
wrong.rationale: Sucrose is a large solute that does not freely cross the membrane; the mass loss reflects water leaving the cells.

wrong.text: Water entered the cells until the cell wall burst, which released fluid into the solution and lowered the mass.
wrong.rationale: Water left the cells in the hypertonic solution; water entry produces firm tissue, not bursting.
wrong.error_pattern: Reverses the direction of water movement

wrong.text: The cells stopped using osmosis in sucrose, so the tissue lost mass through evaporation rather than through water movement.
wrong.rationale: The measured loss arises from net osmosis out of the cells; sucrose does not switch osmosis off.

change_note: New plant tissue and data (sucrose mass change, recomputed -14%) asking why the tissue wilts rather than why it stays intact.

title: Protoplasts burst in water
stem: Plant biologists treat leaf cells with enzymes that digest the cellulose cell wall, producing protoplasts. Intact leaf cells placed in distilled water become firm but stay intact, whereas protoplasts placed in distilled water swell and many burst. Which best explains the difference in outcome?

correct.text: Without a wall, protoplasts have nothing to resist water entering by osmosis, so no turgor pressure limits swelling and the membrane ruptures.
correct.rationale: The wall provides counter-pressure that limits swelling in intact cells; removing it lets water entry continue until the membrane lyses.

wrong.text: The enzyme treatment makes the cytoplasm of protoplasts hypertonic to the intact cells, so water moves out until they burst.
wrong.rationale: Water moving out would shrink the cells; bursting results from net water entry in a hypotonic solution.

wrong.text: Protoplasts lose their plasma membranes during digestion, so distilled water flows freely through them until they rupture.
wrong.rationale: The enzymes digest the cellulose wall, not the plasma membrane, which still bounds the protoplast.
wrong.error_pattern: Believes the wall digestion removes the membrane

wrong.text: Intact cells stay whole because their cytoplasm is isotonic to distilled water, whereas the protoplasts become hypotonic to it.
wrong.rationale: Distilled water is hypotonic to both intact cells and protoplasts; the wall, not an isotonic cytoplasm, prevents bursting.
wrong.error_pattern: Claims intact plant cells are isotonic to water

change_note: Wall-removal experiment (protoplasts) tests the same wall/turgor reasoning with different evidence.

title: Wilting of plants in salty soil
stem: A gardener waters houseplants with a very salty solution. Within hours the leaves droop, and under a microscope the plasma membranes of the leaf cells have pulled away from the cell walls. Plants watered with fresh water stay upright and firm. Which best explains why the plants watered with salty solution droop?

correct.text: Water moved out of the cells by osmosis into the salty surroundings, so the cells lost turgor pressure and the tissue wilted.
correct.rationale: The salty solution is hypertonic to the cells, water leaves, turgor pressure falls, and the membrane pulls from the wall.

wrong.text: Salt entered the cells and made the cell walls swell, which pushed the plasma membranes away from the cell walls.
wrong.rationale: The membrane pulls away because the cytoplasm shrinks as water leaves; salt does not swell the cell wall.

wrong.text: Water moved into the cells until the walls cracked, so the cells became flaccid and the leaves drooped.
wrong.rationale: Water entry would raise turgor and firmness; drooping accompanies water loss.

wrong.text: The cell walls dissolved in the salty solution, so the cells could no longer hold any water and the leaves drooped.
wrong.rationale: Cell walls do not dissolve in salt solution; the cells droop because of osmotic loss of water.

change_note: Flip of seed: loss of turgor in hypertonic conditions in a garden setting.

title: Transferrin receptor deficiency
stem: Developing red blood cells take up iron by receptor-mediated endocytosis. Iron-carrying transferrin in the blood binds to transferrin receptors in the plasma membrane, the membrane folds inward, and a vesicle carries the transferrin into the cell. A patient has a mutation that removes functional transferrin receptors from the cell surface. Which prediction is best supported by the described process?

correct.text: Iron-loaded transferrin will remain in the blood while developing red blood cells receive too little iron, because transferrin cannot bind and be taken in.
correct.rationale: Without receptors the transferrin cannot be recognized or engulfed, so it stays in circulation and the cells lack iron.

wrong.text: The cells will take in transferrin normally through the lipid bilayer, because diffusion of large proteins does not need membrane proteins.
wrong.rationale: Transferrin is a large protein that cannot diffuse across the bilayer; its uptake depends on receptor binding.
wrong.error_pattern: Assumes large proteins diffuse across membranes

wrong.text: The cells will make extra receptors inside vesicles, which will move iron into the cytoplasm without any need for binding.
wrong.rationale: Nothing in the description allows iron to enter without receptor-mediated uptake; vesicles form after binding at the surface.

wrong.text: Transferrin will be engulfed and then trapped in vesicles because the vesicles cannot move to the interior of the cell.
wrong.rationale: Without receptors transferrin is not engulfed, so no vesicles containing it form.

change_note: Different ligand/receptor (transferrin) in a new cell type; same prediction skill with a receptor loss.

title: Blocked vesicle fusion in beta cells
stem: Pancreatic beta cells store insulin in secretory vesicles. When blood glucose rises, the vesicles move to the plasma membrane, fuse with it, and release insulin outside the cell by exocytosis. A toxin prevents secretory vesicles from fusing with the plasma membrane but does not affect insulin synthesis. Which prediction is best supported by the described process?

correct.text: Insulin will build up inside undelivered vesicles, and blood glucose will stay high because little insulin is released from the cells.
correct.rationale: Fusion is required to release insulin, so insulin accumulates in vesicles and glucose remains elevated.

wrong.text: Insulin will diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer instead, so blood glucose will fall at the normal rate.
wrong.rationale: Insulin is a protein too large and polar to diffuse across the bilayer, so release depends on exocytosis.
wrong.error_pattern: Assumes proteins diffuse across the bilayer

wrong.text: Beta cells will stop making insulin completely, because the toxin blocks translation on ribosomes of the rough ER.
wrong.rationale: The toxin affects vesicle fusion, and insulin synthesis is described as unaffected.
wrong.error_pattern: Confuses block of release with block of synthesis

wrong.text: Insulin will be taken up into the cells by endocytosis, which lowers the amount of insulin in the vesicles.
wrong.rationale: Endocytosis moves material into the cell; the toxin affects exocytosis, and import would not reduce stored insulin.

change_note: Exocytosis instead of receptor-mediated endocytosis; same membrane-transport prediction skill.

title: Drug that blocks vesicle formation
stem: Liver cells remove LDL from the blood by receptor-mediated endocytosis. LDL binds to receptors in the plasma membrane, the membrane folds inward, and a vesicle pinches off to carry LDL into the cell. A drug allows LDL to bind to the receptors normally but prevents the membrane from folding inward and pinching off. Which prediction is best supported by the described process?

correct.text: LDL will remain bound to receptors at the cell surface and not enter the cells, so blood LDL will rise.
correct.rationale: Binding is intact but the inward folding is blocked, so LDL is not internalized and is not cleared from the blood.

wrong.text: LDL will not bind to receptors, because the drug stops the folding that makes the receptors able to bind LDL.
wrong.rationale: The drug is described as letting binding occur normally; binding happens before the membrane folds.

wrong.text: LDL will pass through the membrane by diffusion because it is blocked from entering the cell by endocytosis.
wrong.rationale: LDL particles are large and cannot cross the bilayer by diffusion, so blocked endocytosis leaves them outside.

wrong.text: LDL will be taken into vesicles faster than normal, because binding without pinching off concentrates it near the receptors.
wrong.rationale: Without pinching off, vesicles cannot form, so uptake cannot speed up.
wrong.error_pattern: Assumes concentration at receptor increases uptake

change_note: Different step blocked (inward folding after binding) forces reasoning about sequence of the endocytosis steps.

title: Assign osmolarities to cell outcomes
stem: Animal cells without a cell wall, whose cytoplasm has an osmolarity of about 280 mOsm/L, were placed in three unlabeled solutions for 10 minutes. In Solution P, the cells kept their normal shape. In Solution Q, the cells shrank and their surfaces became wrinkled. In Solution R, the cells swelled and about half burst. Which set of osmolarities is most consistent with the outcomes for P, Q, and R respectively?

correct.text: P = 280 mOsm/L; Q = 600 mOsm/L; R = 50 mOsm/L
correct.rationale: P is isotonic so no net water movement; Q is hypertonic so water leaves and the cells shrink; R is hypotonic so water enters and cells swell and lyse.

wrong.text: P = 280 mOsm/L; Q = 50 mOsm/L; R = 600 mOsm/L
wrong.rationale: Q and R are reversed: a 50 mOsm/L solution is hypotonic and would cause swelling, while 600 mOsm/L would cause shrinking.

wrong.text: P = 600 mOsm/L; Q = 280 mOsm/L; R = 50 mOsm/L
wrong.rationale: At 600 mOsm/L the cells would shrink, not stay normal, and at 280 mOsm/L, which is isotonic, they would not shrink.
wrong.error_pattern: Assigns the highest value to normal cells

wrong.text: P = 50 mOsm/L; Q = 280 mOsm/L; R = 600 mOsm/L
wrong.rationale: At 50 mOsm/L the cells would swell and lyse, not remain normal, and 600 mOsm/L would shrink them rather than burst them.
wrong.error_pattern: Assigns lowest value to normal cells

change_note: Different animal-cell cytoplasm value (280) and different symptoms/labels; matching outcomes to osmolarities.

title: Predicting outcomes from osmolarity
stem: Cultured animal cells with no cell wall have a cytoplasmic osmolarity of 300 mOsm/L. The cells are placed in three solutions that contain only solutes unable to cross the plasma membrane: Solution A at 150 mOsm/L, Solution B at 300 mOsm/L, and Solution C at 450 mOsm/L. Which set of outcomes is most likely for the cells in A, B, and C respectively?

correct.text: A: cells swell and may lyse; B: no net change in volume; C: cells lose water and shrink
correct.rationale: A is hypotonic so water enters, B is isotonic so there is no net water movement, and C is hypertonic so water leaves.

wrong.text: A: cells lose water and shrink; B: no net change in volume; C: cells swell and may lyse
wrong.rationale: The outcomes for A and C are swapped: 150 mOsm/L is hypotonic and causes swelling, while 450 mOsm/L is hypertonic and causes shrinking.
wrong.error_pattern: Reverses direction of net water movement

wrong.text: A: no net change in volume; B: cells swell and may lyse; C: cells lose water and shrink
wrong.rationale: B matches the cytoplasm, so it is isotonic and would cause no net change; A is hypotonic and would not leave the cells unchanged.

wrong.text: A: cells swell and may lyse; B: cells lose water and shrink; C: no net change in volume
wrong.rationale: B is isotonic and C is hypertonic, so the cells would not shrink in B or stay unchanged in C.
wrong.error_pattern: Treats the highest solution as isotonic

change_note: Reverse direction (predict outcomes from osmolarity) with impermeant solutes; values recomputed as hypo/iso/hypertonic.

title: Order solutions by osmolarity from volume data
stem: Identical wall-less animal cells were placed in four solutions of non-penetrating solutes for 10 minutes, and the change in cell volume was recorded: Solution 1, +25%; Solution 2, -18%; Solution 3, 0%; Solution 4, -30%. Which ordering of the solutions from lowest to highest osmolarity is most consistent with the data?

correct.text: Solution 1, Solution 3, Solution 2, Solution 4
correct.rationale: The more cells swell, the lower the solution's osmolarity; 0% change marks the isotonic point, and larger shrinkage means higher osmolarity.

wrong.text: Solution 4, Solution 2, Solution 3, Solution 1
wrong.rationale: This is the reverse order; the solution that caused the greatest swelling has the lowest osmolarity, not the highest.
wrong.error_pattern: Reverses the direction of the relationship

wrong.text: Solution 3, Solution 2, Solution 1, Solution 4
wrong.rationale: This ranks by size of volume change, ignoring that swelling and shrinking occur on opposite sides of isotonic.
wrong.error_pattern: Ranks by size of change, ignoring sign

wrong.text: Solution 1, Solution 2, Solution 3, Solution 4
wrong.rationale: This follows the order of the numbers in the list rather than the data; Solution 2 shrank cells, so it exceeds Solution 3.

change_note: Quantitative data table (percent volume change) must be converted into a rank order of osmolarity.

title: Blocked Golgi-to-membrane vesicles in plasma cells
stem: Plasma cells secrete antibodies. Antibodies are made by ribosomes on the rough ER, transferred to the Golgi complex for modification, and carried in vesicles from the Golgi complex to the plasma membrane for secretion. A drug blocks the fusion of those Golgi vesicles with the plasma membrane. Which outcome for antibody is most likely in the treated cells?

correct.text: Antibody is still made and enters the Golgi complex and vesicles, but it accumulates inside the cell and little is secreted.
correct.rationale: Synthesis and processing are intact; blocked fusion leaves the antibody in vesicles and little is released.

wrong.text: Antibody is no longer made, because ribosomes on the rough ER stop translating when vesicles cannot fuse with the membrane.
wrong.rationale: The drug acts on vesicle fusion at the end of the pathway; it does not stop ribosomes from making the protein.
wrong.error_pattern: Confuses a late block with a block of synthesis

wrong.text: Antibody is released from the rough ER directly to the outside of the cell, bypassing the blocked Golgi vesicles.
wrong.rationale: Antibody is not secreted straight from the rough ER; it must be processed in the Golgi complex and carried in vesicles.

wrong.text: Antibody is made by ribosomes in the vesicles instead, and the cells secrete it by a different route.
wrong.rationale: Ribosomes on the rough ER, not those in transport vesicles, make the antibody, and no alternative route is described.
wrong.error_pattern: Invents a new site of synthesis

change_note: Plasma cell antibody secretion with a later block (Golgi vesicle fusion) than the seed's ER-to-Golgi block.

title: Drug blocks lysosomal enzyme packaging
stem: Hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn-out cell components are made by ribosomes on the rough ER, then modified and sorted in the Golgi complex into vesicles that become lysosomes. A drug prevents the Golgi complex from packaging these enzymes into vesicles but does not affect enzyme synthesis. Which outcome is most likely in the treated cells?

correct.text: The enzymes are still made, but they do not reach lysosomes, so worn-out cell components are digested less and accumulate.
correct.rationale: Packaging in the Golgi complex is required to deliver enzymes to lysosomes, so digestion falls and material accumulates.

wrong.text: The enzymes are made inside the lysosomes instead, so worn-out components are digested at the normal rate.
wrong.rationale: Lysosomal enzymes are made at the rough ER; the lysosome receives them and does not make them.

wrong.text: The enzymes are no longer made, because the Golgi complex supplies the ribosomes that carry out their synthesis.
wrong.rationale: Ribosomes make enzymes independent of the Golgi complex, and the drug is stated not to affect synthesis.

wrong.text: The enzymes are digested by the Golgi complex, so worn-out components are broken down faster than in untreated cells.
wrong.rationale: The Golgi complex modifies and packages proteins; it does not digest them or speed up breakdown of cell components.

change_note: Lysosome-bound protein pathway instead of secretion; same ER-Golgi-vesicle sequence logic.

title: Cell type with extensive rough ER and Golgi
stem: A biologist examines four cell types for organelles. Cell W secretes large amounts of a protein hormone. Cell X secretes a steroid hormone, which is a lipid. Cell Y contracts and contains many mitochondria. Cell Z stores fat in a large droplet. Protein destined for secretion is made on the rough ER and then processed by the Golgi complex. Which cell would be expected to have the most extensive rough ER and Golgi complex?

correct.text: Cell W, because making and secreting a large amount of protein depends on the rough ER and Golgi complex.
correct.rationale: A cell that secretes a lot of protein needs many ribosomes on rough ER and extensive Golgi processing and packaging.

wrong.text: Cell X, because lipids such as steroids are made on the rough ER and then secreted in vesicles from the Golgi.
wrong.rationale: Steroid hormones are lipids made by smooth ER, so Cell X would be expected to have extensive smooth ER, not rough ER.
wrong.error_pattern: Confuses rough ER with smooth ER

wrong.text: Cell Y, because the many mitochondria in the cell supply the protein that the rough ER and Golgi complex store.
wrong.rationale: Mitochondria supply ATP and do not make protein for the rough ER and Golgi; a contractile cell does not secrete large amounts of protein.

wrong.text: Cell Z, because a large droplet of fat has to be packaged by the Golgi complex before it can be stored.
wrong.rationale: Stored fat in a droplet is not made or secreted through the rough ER and Golgi pathway, so this cell has little need for them.
wrong.error_pattern: Assumes all storage requires the Golgi

change_note: Application item: matches cell function to organelle abundance instead of predicting a drug outcome; same topic.

title: Chloroplast engulfment evidence
stem: Evidence supporting the endosymbiotic origin of chloroplasts includes: (1) chloroplasts are surrounded by two membranes, with the inner one resembling a bacterial plasma membrane and the outer one resembling the host's membrane; (2) chloroplasts have their own circular DNA; (3) chloroplasts have 70S ribosomes like those of bacteria; (4) chloroplasts divide in a way similar to binary fission. Which single piece of evidence most specifically supports the claim that a prokaryote was taken up by a host cell, rather than just showing prokaryote-like features?

correct.text: The two membranes, with an inner layer like a bacterial plasma membrane and an outer layer like the host, match a prokaryote taken in inside a host membrane.
correct.rationale: The double membrane is the structural result expected if a host cell engulfed a prokaryote in a vesicle.

wrong.text: The circular DNA shows that chloroplasts can still live outside plant cells in the way that free-living bacteria do.
wrong.rationale: Circular DNA shows similarity to prokaryotes; it does not show independence, and chloroplasts depend on their host cells.

wrong.text: The 70S ribosomes show that chloroplasts take in whole bacteria from the environment when plant cells divide.
wrong.rationale: Ribosome type shows similarity to bacteria; it does not describe uptake of bacteria.
wrong.error_pattern: Reads ribosome type as evidence for uptake

wrong.text: The division like binary fission shows that chloroplasts are fully independent prokaryotes that live inside the plant cell.
wrong.rationale: Division resembling binary fission shows prokaryote-like reproduction, but chloroplasts rely on the host and are not independent prokaryotes.

change_note: Chloroplast version of the engulfment-evidence item with distractors tied to genome, ribosomes and division.

title: Additional evidence for endosymbiosis
stem: In an amoeba, researchers find a photosynthetic organelle with two membranes, its own circular DNA, and a division pattern resembling binary fission. They propose that it arose from an engulfed photosynthetic bacterium. Which additional observation would most strongly support the proposal?

correct.text: The organelle's DNA sequence is more similar to that of free-living photosynthetic bacteria than to the amoeba's nuclear DNA.
correct.rationale: A genome closer to a free-living bacterium than to the host nucleus indicates the organelle's ancestor was a separate bacterial lineage.

wrong.text: The organelle contains ribosomes that make protein, since all cells need ribosomes for protein synthesis.
wrong.rationale: Ribosomes occur in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, so their presence does not tie the organelle to a bacterial ancestor.
wrong.error_pattern: Treats universal feature as specific evidence

wrong.text: The organelle's membranes contain phospholipids, which are the molecules that form every cell membrane.
wrong.rationale: Phospholipids are found in all membranes, bacterial and eukaryotic, so they cannot discriminate between the possibilities.
wrong.error_pattern: Treats universal feature as specific evidence

wrong.text: The organelle is found in the cytoplasm of the amoeba, rather than in the nucleus, which shows it came from outside.
wrong.rationale: Many eukaryotic organelles are in the cytoplasm and arise from within the cell, so location does not show an outside origin.

change_note: Asks for the next best supporting observation, with universal features as distractors; different organelle context.

title: Antibiotic prediction from endosymbiosis
stem: Antibiotic Q blocks protein synthesis on 70S ribosomes of bacteria but does not affect the 80S ribosomes found in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells. Mitochondria contain their own ribosomes. If mitochondria arose from engulfed bacteria, which result is most likely when human cells in culture are treated with antibiotic Q?

correct.text: Protein synthesis inside mitochondria is inhibited, while protein synthesis on cytoplasmic ribosomes continues.
correct.rationale: If mitochondrial ribosomes resemble bacterial 70S ribosomes, antibiotic Q blocks them but not the cytoplasmic 80S ribosomes.

wrong.text: Protein synthesis on cytoplasmic ribosomes is inhibited, while mitochondrial protein synthesis continues without change.
wrong.rationale: This reverses the targets: Q affects 70S ribosomes, the type expected in mitochondria, and spares the cytoplasmic 80S ribosomes.

wrong.text: All protein synthesis stops, because the same ribosome type makes protein in the cytoplasm and in mitochondria.
wrong.rationale: The prediction relies on mitochondria having bacteria-like ribosomes that differ from cytoplasmic ribosomes.

wrong.text: No protein synthesis is affected, because mitochondria contain no ribosomes and make no protein of their own.
wrong.rationale: Mitochondria are stated to have their own ribosomes and they do make some of their own proteins.

change_note: Predictive application of endosymbiosis (ribosome type and antibiotic) rather than picking evidence.

title: Channel protein surface chemistry
stem: A transmembrane channel protein forms a pore through the plasma membrane that lets ions pass. Researchers analyze the R groups of its amino acids. Which description of the protein's R groups is most consistent with its location and function?

correct.text: Nonpolar R groups on the outer surface that contacts the phospholipid tails, and polar R groups lining the interior of the pore.
correct.rationale: Nonpolar outer R groups are stable next to hydrophobic tails, while polar R groups lining the pore favor passage of ions and water.

wrong.text: Polar R groups on the outer surface that contacts the phospholipid tails, and nonpolar R groups lining the interior of the pore.
wrong.rationale: This reverses the arrangement: polar groups are unstable beside hydrophobic tails, and nonpolar groups would hinder the passage of ions.

wrong.text: Only nonpolar R groups throughout the protein, since the protein is embedded in the hydrophobic interior of the membrane.
wrong.rationale: A pore lined only with nonpolar R groups would not let ions pass; the pore lining must be polar.
wrong.error_pattern: Treats the entire protein as hydrophobic

wrong.text: Only polar R groups throughout the protein, since the pore carries ions that are dissolved in the water.
wrong.rationale: Polar groups on the outer surface would not be stable next to the hydrophobic phospholipid tails.
wrong.error_pattern: Treats the entire protein as hydrophilic

change_note: Channel with two distinct surfaces (outer lipid-contacting, inner pore) instead of one nonpolar surface.

title: Peripheral protein removed by salt
stem: Researchers study Protein Q from broken red blood cell membranes. Washing the membranes with a high-salt solution releases Protein Q, and the phospholipid bilayer stays intact. The amino acids on the surface of Protein Q have mostly polar and charged R groups. Which characterization of Protein Q is best supported by these results?

correct.text: A protein attached to the membrane surface by interactions between its polar R groups and the polar heads of phospholipids or other membrane proteins.
correct.rationale: Easy removal without dissolving the bilayer and a polar surface indicate a surface-associated protein interacting with polar regions.

wrong.text: A protein embedded in the bilayer, with nonpolar R groups that touch the hydrophobic tails of the phospholipids.
wrong.rationale: An embedded protein with a nonpolar surface would not be released by salt and would require dissolving the bilayer.
wrong.error_pattern: Treats all membrane proteins as embedded

wrong.text: A protein spanning the bilayer, with polar R groups on the surface that touches the phospholipid tails.
wrong.rationale: Polar R groups are not stable next to hydrophobic tails, and a spanning protein would not be released by salt.
wrong.error_pattern: Places polar groups in lipid core

wrong.text: A protein dissolved in the interior of the bilayer, with nonpolar R groups that interact with the surrounding water.
wrong.rationale: Nonpolar R groups do not interact favorably with water, and this protein was released from the surface rather than from the interior.

change_note: Peripheral rather than integral protein; polar surface and gentle release as evidence.

title: Hydrophobic stretches in membrane protein sequence
stem: A researcher determines the amino acid sequence of Protein T. Seven separate stretches of about 20 amino acids each have only nonpolar R groups, and the regions between the stretches have mostly polar R groups. Protein T can be removed from membranes only by dissolving the lipid bilayer with a detergent. Which description of Protein T is best supported by these results?

correct.text: A protein that crosses the bilayer several times, with its nonpolar stretches in the membrane interior and its polar regions outside the bilayer.
correct.rationale: Nonpolar stretches fit among the hydrophobic tails, while polar regions stay in the aqueous environments on either side.

wrong.text: A protein dissolved in the cytoplasm, with its nonpolar stretches facing outward toward the surrounding water.
wrong.rationale: Nonpolar stretches facing water are unstable, and the need for detergent shows Protein T is part of the bilayer, not dissolved.

wrong.text: A protein attached to the outside of the membrane, with its nonpolar stretches facing the watery fluid around it.
wrong.rationale: Removal requires dissolving the bilayer, so the protein is not simply attached outside, and nonpolar stretches would not face water.

wrong.text: A protein with all of its polar regions buried in the center of the bilayer, among the hydrophobic tails.
wrong.rationale: Polar regions are not stable among the hydrophobic tails; the nonpolar stretches belong there.
wrong.error_pattern: Places polar groups in lipid core

change_note: Inference from primary sequence pattern (nonpolar stretches) plus detergent evidence to membrane-spanning protein.

title: GLUT4 insertion and blood glucose
stem: GLUT4 is a glucose transport protein in muscle cells. When insulin is released after a meal, vesicles containing GLUT4 fuse with the plasma membrane within minutes, and the number of GLUT4 channels at the membrane increases about 8-fold. Glucose then enters the cell down its concentration gradient without ATP use. In mice lacking functional GLUT4 insertion, blood glucose stays high after a meal. Which chain of reasoning correctly connects the cellular change to the whole-organism outcome in wild-type mice?

correct.text: Insulin → GLUT4 vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane → more glucose channels → glucose moves into muscle cells by facilitated diffusion → blood glucose falls
correct.rationale: Insulin inserts GLUT4 into the membrane, glucose enters passively down its gradient, and blood glucose is lowered.

wrong.text: Insulin → GLUT4 is removed from the plasma membrane → fewer glucose channels → glucose leaves muscle cells → blood glucose falls
wrong.rationale: Insulin adds GLUT4 to the membrane; removing channels would resemble the mutant mice, whose blood glucose stays high.

wrong.text: Insulin → GLUT4 vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane → GLUT4 pumps glucose into the cell using ATP against its gradient → blood glucose falls
wrong.rationale: The description states glucose enters down its gradient without ATP, so GLUT4 works by facilitated diffusion, not active transport.

wrong.text: Insulin → GLUT4 vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane → glucose passes into the cell directly through the phospholipids → blood glucose falls
wrong.rationale: Glucose is polar and cannot cross the bilayer quickly; it enters through GLUT4, which is why mice without insertion stay hyperglycemic.
wrong.error_pattern: Assumes glucose diffuses across the bilayer

change_note: Different transporter (GLUT4, facilitated diffusion) and organism context; chain from membrane change to whole-organism outcome.

title: CFTR chloride channel and airway mucus
stem: CFTR is a chloride channel in the plasma membrane of airway epithelial cells. Chloride ions flow out through CFTR down their electrochemical gradient into the thin liquid layer covering the cells, and water then follows by osmosis. In people with CFTR mutations that prevent the channel from reaching the membrane, the liquid layer is thin and the mucus is thick and sticky. Which chain of reasoning correctly connects the cellular change to the tissue-level outcome in people with normal CFTR?

correct.text: CFTR is in the membrane → chloride moves out through the channel → the liquid layer becomes more concentrated → water moves in by osmosis → mucus stays thin
correct.rationale: Channels let chloride exit, raising solute concentration outside the cells, so water follows and mucus stays hydrated.

wrong.text: CFTR is in the membrane → chloride moves into the cells → the outside liquid becomes more dilute → water moves out of the layer → mucus becomes thick
wrong.rationale: Normal CFTR moves chloride out, not in, and a dilute layer would pull water away, producing thick mucus like the mutant case.

wrong.text: CFTR is in the membrane → water moves out of the cells first → chloride is dragged along with the water → mucus stays thin
wrong.rationale: Water follows solute by osmosis; it does not move first and pull chloride, so the chain order is wrong.
wrong.error_pattern: Reverses order of solute and water movement

wrong.text: CFTR is in the membrane → chloride is held inside the cells → the liquid layer becomes less concentrated → mucus stays thin
wrong.rationale: A channel allows chloride to leave; holding it inside would leave the outside layer dilute, as in thick mucus.

change_note: Chloride channel and osmotic water movement in airway cells; new organism, new reasoning chain.

title: AQP1 knockout red blood cells swell slowly
stem: Red blood cells contain aquaporin-1 (AQP1) channels. When wild-type red blood cells are moved into a hypotonic solution, they swell and lyse in about 20 seconds. Red blood cells from mice lacking AQP1 also swell and lyse in the same solution, but only after about 60 seconds, which is 3 times as long as the wild type. The solutions and internal osmolarities are identical in both groups. Which explanation best accounts for the difference?

correct.text: Without AQP1, water still crosses by diffusing through the phospholipid bilayer, but more slowly, so the cells swell and lyse after a longer time.
correct.rationale: Aquaporins speed water movement; without them, osmosis still occurs across the bilayer, but at a lower rate.

wrong.text: Without AQP1, water cannot cross the plasma membrane, so the knockout cells swell only because solutes enter them over time.
wrong.rationale: The knockout cells lyse in a hypotonic solution, which requires water entry, so water still crosses the membrane.
wrong.error_pattern: Believes water cannot cross the bilayer

wrong.text: AQP1 channels use ATP to push water into the cell, so cells lacking them have less energy to draw in water.
wrong.rationale: Water moves by osmosis down its gradient; aquaporins are passive channels that do not use ATP.

wrong.text: The knockout cells have a lower internal solute concentration, so the osmotic gradient is smaller and swelling is slower.
wrong.rationale: The problem states that the solutions and internal osmolarities are identical, so the gradient is the same in both groups.

change_note: Knockout data with recomputed 3x ratio; tests that aquaporins change rate not direction or energy source.
